newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh government faces tough budget test.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh government faces tough budget test.

text.p: Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's government faces a tough call by analysts to cut costs, raise revenues and avoid new taxes in the new budget for the 1997/98 fiscal year beginning on July 1.
The government's dilemma could be complicated by recent demands from employees in the government secretariat for new pay scales which might double salaries, analysts said.
The new pay scales, which would be effective from July 1, could boost expenditure by about 15 billion taka ($343 million) and may fuel inflation, government officials say.
Private economists say the government must cut expenditure and avoid fresh taxes in the new budget, expected to be announced on June 12.
They say the tax base should be expanded through effective fiscal management rather than raising taxes.
Finance ministry officials have said the government planned to raise up to seven billion taka in additional revenue through expansion of the Value Added Tax (VAT) coverage.

Also, the government has been under pressure from international donors since it took power in June last year, to raise prices of utilities, privatise loss-making public companies and lower import tariffs.
Finance ministry officials have said that the government might project a budget surplus for 1997/98 with a forecast of more than 200 billion taka in revenue and over 140 billion in expenditure.

The budget for 1996/97 (July-June), which had been projected at a surplus of 37 billion taka, was now likely to be balanced, the officials said. The revenue target had been set at 155.12 billion taka against expenditure of 118.14 billion.

A senior official said revenue was now expected at 130.4 billion taka while expenditure might have overshot the target by about four billion taka. The officials said the budget had set ambitious targets.
Banking sources said the government's internal debt had risen and that had contributed to lower investment in the country this year.
"The government borrowing from banks could be more than 12 billion taka," one bank official said. Government internal debt stood at 15 billion taka in 1995/96.

Atiur Rahman, a senior research fellow with the Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies, said excessive government borrowings had restricted funding to the private sector. He said the government should create a separate credit line for giving long-term industrial loans.
"The banking sector is in difficulties and it needs fresh doses of liquidity to finance industrial projects. Such provision of funds should be made in the new budget."
The country's banking sector is teetering under the weight of about 130 billion taka in outstanding loans, which has hit industrial growth particularly hard.
Government officials expect industrial growth to be lower in 1996/97 than the 6.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) growth rate in 1995/96.

Yusuf Abdullah Haroon, President of the Federation of Bangladesh Chamber of Commerce and Industry said the government should lower the corporate tax rate for listed companies in the new budget to boost industrialisation.
The corporate tax rate for listed companies is 35 percent and 40 percent for unlisted companies.
Kazi Koliquzzaman Ahmed, Chairman of the Bangladesh Development Council, a think-tank, said Bangladesh must raise its GDP growth to fight poverty.
"Investment could help boost the growth. But we need political stability and establishment of rule of law in the country to attract both domestic and foreign investment," he told Reuters.

Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria said the country expected higher GDP growth at 5.7 percent in 1996/97. The government plans to set the growth target at 6.0 percent for 1997/98, he told Reuters in an interview recently.
He said the government would achieve higher growth by maintaining budgetary balance, reducing government expenditure and increasing private sector credit.
Bangladesh receives nearly $1.8 billion in annual foreign aid to finance development and imports. The country's annual per capita income is only $240. ($1 = 43.76 taka)
